headline: 3 memory changes experts warn you should never ignore as you’re aging
author: Christy Bieber

paragraphs.text: Dementia is a leading cause of death globally as well as a growing problem in America due to an aging population. Over 6 million Americans suffer from dementia, according to research published by the National Institutes of Health, and an estimated 42 percent of men and women over 55 are expected to eventually develop the condition.

“Early detection of dementia-related illnesses is essential,” said Jeremy Koppel, a medical advisory board member at the Alzheimer’s Foundation of America and co-director of the Litwin-Zucker Research Center for the Study of Alzheimer’s Disease, in New York. “Delays in diagnosis can mean missed opportunities.”

But dementia isn’t the only health issue that affects memory. Sleep apnea, thyroid disorders, depression, urinary tract infections and vitamin deficiencies are just some of the many conditions that can cause memory impairments, Koppel said. Many of these issues are treatable.
Because some forgetfulness is normal as people age, it’s often hard to know if a memory lapse is cause for concern. Medical experts say these particular symptoms deserve attention.
1. Changes that make daily life harder
When it comes to distinguishing ordinary forgetfulness from a potentially serious problem, experts say one key factor matters.

“The question isn’t simply whether you forget things. It’s whether your memory changes are making daily life harder,” said Anna Chodos, a geriatrician and professor of medicine at the University of California at San Francisco.

Michael Leon, professor emeritus of neurobiology and behavior at the University of California at Irvine, agreed, warning that while occasional forgetfulness like misplacing keys or taking longer to recall a name is common, “changes that interfere with daily self-care or safety go beyond normal aging.”

Leon gave multiple examples of lapses that fall into this category, including forgetting which medications to take or missing doses, struggling to cook a recipe you’ve made for years, or suddenly being unable to use your phone correctly.

“This progressive loss of everyday skills is often one of the most noticeable effects on daily life,” said Emer MacSweeney, a neuroradiologist and CEO of Re:Cognition Health, which operates clinics focused on cognitive health care in London and several U.S. locations, including Virginia and Chicago.
2. Forgetting how to have a conversation
Memory changes that affect your ability to communicate are another red flag that experts suggest paying attention to.

“Changes I’d encourage people not to ignore include repeatedly asking the same question or forgetting recent conversations,” Chodos said. Christine Ghilain, a neuropsychologist and neuropsychological evaluator in New Jersey, said it’s a red flag if you find yourself “frequently losing words or losing the thread of a conversation.”

Friends and family members are often the first to notice these types of changes, which makes it important to listen when someone close to you expresses concern. “If a loved one is worried, take it seriously. People often don’t realize how much they’ve adapted to their changes,” said Ghilain.
3. Difficulty remembering recent events

Alzheimer’s, which is the most common type of dementia, often affects short-term memory first, while long-term memories may not begin to fade until the disease has progressed. That’s why Koppel says it’s a cause for concern if you’re having difficulty recalling things that should be fresh in your mind.
As Koppel explained, this is called episodic memory loss, and it’s often one of the earliest and most defining signs of Alzheimer’s disease.

Episodic memory is the type that allows you to recall basic personal experiences, like what you ate for lunch and where you parked. It records the who, what, where, when and why of your day. A neurodegenerative condition can result in these things not being properly recorded in the brain.

Forgetting recent events, especially when reminders don’t help, can indicate your brain is having difficulty forming or retaining new memories due to a medical issue, rather than just ordinary forgetfulness, said Jordan Weiss, an assistant professor at NYU Grossman School of Medicine’s Optimal Aging Institute.
Take swift action if you see these signs

If these warning signs are familiar, visiting your doctor could make a substantial difference in your long-term health, as early evaluation may uncover a treatable condition or provide opportunities to better manage an irreversible diagnosis.

“Not all memory loss is permanent dementia,” Leon said. “Symptoms can be triggered by reversible conditions, such as vitamin B12 deficiency, thyroid imbalances, medication side effects, infections, sleep apnea or depression. Identifying these root causes early can restore full memory function.”

If dementia is the likely cause, swift action is imperative. Koppel warned that many medications for Alzheimer’s disease are effective, or even available, only in the early stage of the disease’s progression, while clinical trials are often limited to early-stage participants.

Anti-amyloid immunotherapies, for example, are often used for early-stage Alzheimer’s to clear amyloid plaques from brain tissue. They may slow disease progression by roughly 20 percent to 40 percent when administered in the earliest stages of the condition.

While it may seem intimidating to see a doctor about these issues, “the goal isn’t to create worry,” Ghilain said. “The goal is to get a clear answer sooner so that people have the best chance to get the right support.”
